full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the order dated 7-9-85 passed by the District Judge, Bakerganj in Title Appeal No. 73 of 1985 rejecting the memo of appeal preferred against the ex parte judgment and decree dated 16-4-1985 and 20-4-1985 respectively passed by the Subordinate Judge. Barisal in Title Suit No. 285 of 1971. 

 3. The petitioner filed an application on 27-6-1984 in that suit under Order XXII, rule 10 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for being added as defendant in the suit as an assignee of the defendant No.5 contending, inter alia, that the defendant No. 5 sold the suit land to Bimal Chandra on 16-3-1974 and the latter sold the same to different persons including the petitioner on 3-6-1974. The said application dated 27-6-1984 was fixed for hearing on 27-8-1984 and the petitioner was ready for hearing filing hazira but when the matter was called on for hearing the learned Advocate for the petitioner could not be present since he was engaged in another Court and ultimately the application was rejected on 27-8-1984. Subsequently it transpired that the said Title Suit No. 285 of 1971 was transformed as Title Suit No. 285 of 1981 in the cause list by the interested party and ultimately the application was rejected on 7-4-1985. The petitioner then again tiled another application under Order XXII, rule 10 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 13-4-1985 stating all the facts in detail but it was rejected on 15-4-1985 and the learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on 16-4-1985. The petitioner then tiled Title Appeal No. 73 of 1985 before the learned District Judge, Bakerganj who by order dated 7-9-1985 rejected the memo of appeal most unjustly. That the petitioner being an assignee of the defendant No.5 is entitled to file the appeal against the decree passed against the defendant No.5 by reason of section 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure. That the rejection of the memo of appeal in question was made not in accordance with law and thereby caused miscarriage of justice to the petitioner and, as such, the impugned order is liable to be set aside. 

 5. Perused the revisional application, the impugned order, the impugned judgment and decree of the trial Court and other papers filed along with the revisional application. 

 6. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that scope has, been provided under section 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure to the petitioner to prefer the aforesaid appeal No. 73 of 1985 as assignee of defendant No.5 and that the petitioner would suffer a colossal loss if he is not allowed to prefer the appeal in question against the judgment and decree dated 16-4-1985 respectively passed by the Subordinate Judge, Barisal in Title Suit No. 285 of 1971. Mr Choudhury, the learned Advocate in appreciation of his submission has cited the decisions in the case of Indomoti Howlader vs ADC and others reported in 50 DLR 444, in the case of Delwar Hossain vs Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 50 DLR 494 and in the case of HM Saya and Co vs Wajir Ali industries Ltd and Habib Bank Limited reported in 21 DLR (SC) 50. 

 8. The learned Advocate submits that it is a fact that the petitioner did not prefer for any relief against the order rejecting his application under Order XXII, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure passed by the trial Court but that does not debar him from preferring an appeal as a stranger as provided under section 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He further submits that after rejection of such application under Order XXII, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the petitioner he has become a third party and sections 96, 104 and 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure do not prohibit a 3rd party/stranger from filing an appeal having interest in the property involved in the proceeding if his interest is adversely affected by an order or decree. 

 9. Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure deals with appeals from decrees and section 104 of the Code of Civil Procedure deals with appeals from orders. This provision does not in terms say who is entitled to prefer an appeal. The Code, however, lays down that it is the decree or the order that has to be appealed against. If the decree or order appealed from adversely affects a person he should be permitted to challenge the same in appeal even if he was not made a party to the original suit or proceeding. The Court should proceed on the principle that every procedure which furthers administration of justice is permissible even if there is no express provision permitting the same. This view finds support from the decision in the case of HM Saya and Co vs Wazid Ali industries Ltd reported in 21 DLR(SC) 50. 

 10. The learned Advocate further submits that the petitioner, as an assignee of the defendant No.5, having interest in the suit property although by rejecting his application under Order XXII, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not allowed to be impleaded as a party to the suit, yet his avenue to prefer an appeal against the judgment and decree in respect of the property having his interest therein is open as provided under section 146 read with section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 11. Considering all the above aspects of the matter and the impugned order, applications under Order XXII, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the petitioner in the trial Court as well as the submissions of the learned Advocate, I find merit in this Rule and hold that the petitioner as the assignee of defendant No, 5 claiming interest in the suit property may file an appeal as a third party or stranger though he was not a party in the suit if his interest is affected by an order or a decree as was asserted to have been caused by the impugned judgment and decree, As such, the impugned order  is not sustainable in the eye of law. Apart from the decision reported in 21 DLR (SC) 50 this view also finds support from the decisions reported in 50 DLR,444 and 54 DLR 494 as referred to above.
